name: Prague Spring
info: The Prague Spring was a period of political liberalisation and mass protest in Czechoslovakia, from Alexander Dubček's election as Communist Party leader on 5 January 1968 to the Warsaw Pact invasion of 21 August 1968 that suppressed the reforms.

facts.where: The Czechoslovak Socialist Republic, above all Prague, Bratislava and Wenceslas Square; the talks were held at Čierna nad Tisou and Bratislava, and Dubček was taken to Moscow after the invasion.
facts.period: Slow de-Stalinisation under Antonín Novotný (late 1950s and 1960s); Dubček became First Secretary on 5 January 1968; the Action Programme of April 1968; talks at Čierna nad Tisou (29 July to 1 August) and the Bratislava Declaration (3 August); invasion on the night of 20–21 August 1968; normalisation from April 1969.
facts.figures: Alexander Dubček, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia; Ludvík Svoboda, who became President in March; the reformers Josef Smrkovský, Oldřich Černík and František Kriegel; the hardliners Vasil Biľak, Drahomír Kolder and Oldřich Švestka; Eduard Goldstücker, head of the Writers' Union; the economist Ota Šik; Leonid Brezhnev for the Soviet Union; Gustáv Husák, who replaced Dubček in 1969.
facts.outcome: The Warsaw Pact invasion ended the reforms. Gustáv Husák reversed almost all of them in a period of normalisation, and only the federalisation of the country into Czech and Slovak republics survived. Czechoslovakia remained a Soviet satellite state until the Velvet Revolution of 1989.

t: Alexander Dubček's Action Programme of April 1968 promised freedom of the press, speech and movement, a partial decentralisation of the economy and a federal Czechoslovakia, under the continued leadership of the Communist Party, in what he called "socialism with a human face".

The Soviet Union tried negotiations at Čierna nad Tisou and Bratislava, and then, on the night of 20–21 August 1968, troops from the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Poland and Hungary occupied the country; Dubček called on his people not to resist, and the resistance that followed was largely nonviolent.

Under Gustáv Husák, normalisation reversed almost all of the reforms from 1969; the federalisation of the country was the only formal change to survive, and the memory of 1968 stayed contested for decades.
dyk: By August 1968 the censor-free journal Literární listy had a circulation of 300,000, making it the most published periodical in Europe.
ev: Marxist intellectuals organise the Liblice Conference on Franz Kafka, which marks the start of the cultural democratisation of Czechoslovakia
At the Writers' Congress in June, Ludvík Vaculík, Milan Kundera and Antonín Liehm deliver speeches against the regime's control of literature

sections.background:
The de-Stalinisation of Czechoslovakia began under Antonín Novotný in the late 1950s and early 1960s but progressed more slowly than in most other states of the Eastern Bloc. Following Nikita Khrushchev, Novotný proclaimed the "completion of socialism", and the new constitution renamed the country the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic. The victims of the Stalin era, such as those convicted in the Slánský trial, were not rehabilitated until 1967. In the early 1960s the economy turned down: the Soviet model of industrialisation applied poorly to a country that had already been quite industrialised before the Second World War, and Novotný's New Economic Model of 1965 increased demand for political reform.

Culture opened first. In May 1963 Marxist intellectuals organised the Liblice Conference on the life of Franz Kafka, who had been heavily criticised in the Eastern Bloc; it led to a partial opening of the regime and a relaxation of censorship, and it made Kafka a symbol of the revival of Czechoslovak artistic and intellectual freedom. Delegates from every Eastern Bloc country were invited, but the Soviet Union sent none.

At the Writers' Congress of June 1967 a small part of the Union of Czechoslovak Writers, among them Ludvík Vaculík, Milan Kundera, Jan Procházka, Antonín Jaroslav Liehm, Pavel Kohout and Ivan Klíma, sympathised with radical socialists. Party leaders decided on administrative action against such writers, and control of the union's weekly Literární noviny passed to the Ministry of Culture, a move endorsed even by some later reformers, including Dubček.
sections.aims:
Alexander Dubček's reforms were an attempt to grant additional rights to the citizens of Czechoslovakia through a partial decentralisation of the economy and a democratisation of political life. The freedoms to be granted included looser restrictions on the media, speech and travel. In April 1968 Dubček launched an Action Programme, which also stressed consumer goods in the economy, spoke of the possibility of a multiparty government and promised to limit the power of the secret police. It took the view that "Socialism cannot mean only liberation of the working people from the domination of exploiting class relations, but must make more provisions for a fuller life of the personality than any bourgeois democracy."

The programme provided for the federalisation of the country into two equal nations, and its foreign policy combined good relations with Western countries and cooperation with the Soviet Union and the rest of the Eastern Bloc. It described a ten-year transition after which democratic elections would be possible and a new democratic socialism would replace the status quo. Its drafters were careful not to criticise the actions of the post-war Communist regime, only to point out policies that had outlived their usefulness. Dubček announced a political programme of "socialism with a human face" and, to meet the declining competitiveness of Czechoslovak exports, planned to mix planned and market economies.

Reform was to proceed under Communist Party direction, and Dubček repeatedly stressed this, but popular pressure mounted to carry it out at once.
sections.events:
Alexander Dubček, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Slovakia, and the economist Ota Šik challenged Novotný at a meeting of the Central Committee. Novotný invited Leonid Brezhnev to Prague in December 1967, but Brezhnev, surprised by the extent of the opposition, supported his removal. Dubček replaced him as First Secretary on 5 January 1968, and on 22 March Novotný resigned as President and was replaced by Ludvík Svoboda. Under the scholar Eduard Goldstücker, Literární noviny became Literární listy, and on 29 February the Writers' Union published the first copy of the censor-free journal. The press began to investigate the Stalinist past.

The Soviet leadership and its allies grew uneasy. At Dresden on 23 March the "Warsaw Five" questioned the Czechoslovak delegation, and in May the KGB began Operation Progress, in which agents infiltrated pro-democratic organisations. Talks with almost the full Soviet Politburo took place at Čierna nad Tisou from 29 July to 1 August, where the Czechoslovak side was divided between reformers (Smrkovský, Černík and Kriegel) and hardliners (Biľak, Kolder and Švestka). Brezhnev chose compromise; on 3 August the Bratislava Declaration affirmed fidelity to Marxism-Leninism and the Soviet Union's intention to intervene if a "bourgeois" system was ever established.

On the night of 20–21 August, 165,000 troops and 4,600 tanks of the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Poland and Hungary entered the country. Dubček was arrested and taken to Moscow, where he and all the highest-ranked leaders but František Kriegel signed the Moscow Protocol.
sections.people:
Alexander Dubček, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Slovakia, replaced Antonín Novotný as First Secretary of the party on 5 January 1968. Beside him the reformers Josef Smrkovský, Oldřich Černík and František Kriegel pressed for change, while Vasil Biľak, Drahomír Kolder and Oldřich Švestka took an anti-reformist stance; more recent evidence indicates that conservatives including Biľak, Švestka, Kolder, Indra and Antonín Kapek sent the Soviets a request for intervention. Ludvík Svoboda became President in March and later gave consent to the reforms. Ota Šik was the economist who challenged Novotný with Dubček.

Writers and journalists carried the movement into public life. Eduard Goldstücker, chairman of the Union of Czechoslovak Writers, criticised Novotný in a television interview on 4 February and suffered no repercussions. Jaroslav Seifert headed the committee on persecuted writers, and Ludvík Vaculík, Milan Kundera, Pavel Kohout and Jan Procházka were among the voices of the cultural opposition. Television brought meetings between writers, political victims such as Smrkovský, Zdeněk Hejzlar and Gustáv Husák, and young workers and students, which moved the political dialogue from the intellectuals to the popular sphere.

On the Soviet side Leonid Brezhnev, Alexei Kosygin, Nikolai Podgorny and Mikhail Suslov negotiated with Dubček. Hungary's János Kádár was at first highly supportive of Dubček's appointment, while Władysław Gomułka and Kádár worried more about the growing criticism in the Czechoslovak media.
sections.outcomes:
The invasion was followed by a wave of emigration: an estimated 70,000 citizens fled at once and some 300,000 in all. People were killed and wounded during the invasion, and Warsaw Pact troops attacked Radio Prague and Czechoslovak Television soon after entering Prague. Dubček had called upon his people not to resist, but there was scattered resistance: road signs were removed or painted over, villages renamed themselves "Dubček" or "Svoboda", and civilians gave wrong directions to soldiers. The generalised resistance led the Soviet Union to give up its original plan to remove the First Secretary. On 16 January 1969 the student Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square to protest against the renewed suppression of free speech.

In April 1969 Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček, who was expelled from the party and given a job as a forestry official. Husák reversed Dubček's reforms, purged the party of its liberal members, dismissed professional and intellectual elites who had openly disagreed, reinstated the power of the police and sought to re-centralise the economy. Press freedom ended in stages: a limited censorship office was agreed in the weeks after the invasion, a new censorship law followed in September 1968, and full censorship was instituted in March 1969. Many of those purged later became dissidents active in Charter 77. The only significant change that survived was the federalisation of the country, which created the Czech Socialist Republic and the Slovak Socialist Republic in 1969.
sections.legacy:
Abroad, most governments offered only vocal criticism. Canada, Denmark, France, Paraguay, the United Kingdom and the United States requested a meeting of the United Nations Security Council, where the Soviet ambassador Jacob Malik called the invasion "fraternal assistance"; a resolution of condemnation was opposed by the Soviet Union, which held a veto. Romania and Albania refused to take part in the invasion, and Albania withdrew from the Warsaw Pact. China condemned the Brezhnev Doctrine, under which the Soviet Union claimed the right to decide which nations were properly Communist. In the West the Prague Spring deepened the disillusionment of many leftists with Soviet views and contributed to the growth of Eurocommunist ideas.

In 1987 Mikhail Gorbachev acknowledged that glasnost and perestroika owed much to Dubček's "socialism with a human face"; asked the difference between the two, a Foreign Ministry spokesman answered, "Nineteen years." Dubček supported the Velvet Revolution of December 1989 and became chairman of the federal assembly under Václav Havel. The last Soviet troops left Czechoslovakia in 1991.

The memory is described as conflicted. The Prague Spring is rarely commemorated in Prague and is often seen as a painful defeat, and history textbooks treat it as one of the major crises of socialism in the Soviet bloc. Others emphasise its cultural impact and the revitalisation of society. The debate resumed in the 2000s, and when the fiftieth anniversary came, the Czech President Miloš Zeman refused to attend any ceremony.

summary: The Prague Spring was the period from January to August 1968 in which Alexander Dubček's reformist leadership loosened press, speech and travel restrictions in Czechoslovakia. Warsaw Pact troops invaded on 21 August; Gustáv Husák reversed almost all the reforms, and only federalisation survived.

notes: The article contradicts itself on how many Warsaw Pact states invaded: the lead names five (adding East Germany), the invasion section says four (Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Poland, Hungary) and that East German troops were not used. The four are used.

Deaths: the invasion section gives 72 killed (19 in Slovakia), 266 severely wounded, 436 slightly injured; the last section says 137 Czechoslovaks died. The article contradicts itself, so no figure is used; the editor may choose one.
The lead says resistance held out for almost eight months and that the Soviet military predicted four days; left out as the body does not explain it.

Dubček is first described as First Secretary of the Communist Party of Slovakia; the article also gives Novotný as President and First Secretary. Novotný's resignation (22 March) is as the article gives it.
The article gives the Warsaw Pact troop figures as 165,000 men and 4,600 tanks on the night, and elsewhere half a million (the New York Times: 650,000); only the first is used.

Left out: the popular-culture list (songs, films, novels, hockey number), the Soviet demonstration in Red Square, and the Radio Free Europe testimonies. The article's sentence that the movement's memory is subject to 'historical amnesia' is not used.
'normalisation' is the article's term (normalizace); British spelling used. The article's 'Dubcek' without the caron appears in places; Dubček used throughout.
The dyk (circulation of 300,000) is the article's figure for Literární listy by August 1968.
